en: The Sūtra on the Questions of King Prasenajit,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court-Attendant of the Third Rank,
Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma.
Translated by the Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a great king named Jayasena in the kingdom of Kośala. This king was noble and possessed great majesty, wealth, and sovereignty; his realm and territory were vast and far-reaching, and he was held in universal respect by all people.
Having long possessed merit and virtue, the king had conceived a profound faith and reverence for the Buddha-dharma.

At that time, the Great King mounted his precious chariot and, surrounded by his ministers and retinue as well as countless hundreds of thousands of brahmins, elders, and others, with various musical instruments leading the way, departed from the city of Śrāvastī and proceeded to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, where the World-Honored Buddha resided; there he paid respectful homage and made offerings, listening to and receiving the True Dharma.
At that time, as a sovereign of the people, he always governed and transformed the realm through the True Dharma, renouncing and refraining from all that was contrary to the Dharma. Why was this?

"Great King, you should know this: if a king and his ministers abandon the True Dharma and practice what is contrary to the Dharma, they will be despised and slandered by people in this present life, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, they will not be reborn in an exalted state.

Conversely, if a king and his ministers renounce what is contrary to the Dharma and practice the True Dharma, they will be praised by people in this present life, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, they will be reborn in the celestial realms to experience superior karmic fruits—abounding in wealth, joy, and sovereignty, and being cherished and honored by devas."

"Great King! It is like a person in the world who gives birth to an only son; his parents cherish and love him as if he were a precious jewel, employing many skillful means to ensure he is always happy. When the son grows up, he likewise develops filial piety and respect. Your Majesty’s compassionate love is just like this: you regard all your people as your only child, and they cherish and honor you as their own parents. You constantly transform and guide them through the four methods—namely, giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation—and because you constantly practice these four kinds of dharmas, all your people submit to you."
The king, with a heart of compassion, regards all his subjects as if they were his own children; likewise, all those people regard the king as their own father or mother.

Furthermore, it is like a person who, within a dream, sees various things—namely, rivers, streams, springs, and ponds; gardens, groves, flowers, and fruits; streets, roads, and pathways, all magnificently adorned, pure, delightful, and pleasing to the senses. Once awakened from the dream, none of these things exist at all. All worldly phenomena are just like this: they are entirely like dreams and ultimately lack any reality.

"O Great King, as you are the sovereign among men, you enjoy three kinds of pleasure: namely, the pleasure of wealth, the pleasure of desire, and the pleasure of sovereignty. You govern a great kingdom and city possessing many things—elephants, horses, chariots, gold, silver, precious gems, and all manner of goods in the treasuries; even your queens, consorts, retinues, ministers, and servants are exceedingly numerous. Though your wealth and nobility are so flourishing and peerless, and though you possess such abundance, you do not consider yourself superior because of them."
Why is this? Because these inverted dharmas weary the mind and increase all manner of afflictions.
"Great King, you should know that all these are dharmas subject to impermanence and extinction; they are not solid and are not ultimate, being like a mass of foam upon water and devoid of reality."
Therefore, Great King!
Understand such matters as they truly are; remain constantly awakened to the phenomena of the world, and cultivate supramundane practice by remaining free from all afflictions.

"Furthermore, worldly dharmas are like a great tree: when its roots are nourished and moistened, branches and leaves grow; when the branches and leaves flourish, it is able to produce flowers; once the flowers have bloomed, before long they bear fruit. When the fruit is ripe, its color and fragrance are exquisite, and all people delight in them."

Suddenly, that tree was consumed by a great fire; it blazed fiercely on all four sides, its crimson flames and radiant light eclipsing the sun and moon, so that in the four directions, above, and below, there was but one great radiance.

Those lovely trees have all vanished, and only the glow of fire appears; yet that fire does not last long before it is extinguished by a great rain, while clouds, thunder, and flashing lightning emerge, illuminating one another.
At that time, the mass of fire completely vanished, and only that great rain continued to pour down incessantly; yet before long, that rain also ceased.

Your Majesty should know that all worldly phenomena previously described are likewise thus: they perish in an instant and possess no ultimate reality. Just as that which you govern, though vast and accumulated, perishes in an instant—the same principle applies to its meaning.
Therefore, Great King!

Do not conceive the notion of permanence regarding impermanent phenomena; do not form the notion of inexhaustibility regarding phenomena that are subject to exhaustion. Contemplate at every moment that impermanence is encroaching; abandon worldly dharmas, detach from all attachments, cultivate supramundane practices, and increase your roots of goodness.

"Great King! Furthermore, it is as if four great mountains were to come from the sky from the four directions; those mountains are high and broad, each one solid and firm, and they fall upon Jambudvīpa. Thereupon, all the grasses, trees, thickets, and forests within this land are utterly crushed and destroyed without remainder, such that even those with great power cannot provide rescue."
"Great King!
It is likewise with these four great terrors that come to oppress all the worlds; there is no place for any sentient being to escape them, and even those of great power cannot provide rescue."
What are the four fears?
First, the fear of wrong conduct;
second, the fear of old age.
Third, the fear of illness;
fourth, the fear of death.
Great King!

If misconduct arises, it destroys right conduct; if the fear of old age comes, it destroys the signs of youth; if the fear of illness comes, it destroys the dharma of well-being; and if the fear of death comes, it destroys and extinguishes life.
Great King!

Furthermore, it is like a lion, the king of beasts; if it enters a herd of animals to seize one for food, how could that seized animal possibly escape? Once it has entered the lion’s belly, it is extinguished without remainder.
"Great King!
The great power of impermanence acts upon all sentient beings in exactly this same way. Great King!"

When people of the world are about to reach the end of their lives, they are first afflicted by the suffering of illness; like those struck by a poisoned arrow, their physical strength is weakened, their sinews, bones, and limbs all ache with pain, their skin and flesh wither away, and their hands and feet tremble. Filth flows out from them, and their faculties—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body—can no longer give rise to consciousness. External objects do not appear before them; instead, only the objects of the unwholesome karma they themselves have created manifest before them. They give rise to great terror, having no one to rely upon or take refuge in—who will be their savior?

Surrounded by parents and kinsmen, though skilled physicians and excellent medicines cannot heal him, and though foods of the finest flavor cannot be consumed, he gives rise to fear of impermanence in every moment of thought. As his inhalations and exhalations gradually become fainter, through this terror of illness, he finally begins to conceive the thought of performing virtuous deeds. With a feeble voice, he addresses his parents, saying: "I am now in great terror;

evil states have appeared before me, and my life is about to end. Parents, for my sake, perform all manner of beneficial acts; bestow offerings upon the Buddha and the Sangha, and I pray you grant me protection."
Having spoken thus, his life was severed in an instant; having passed away from this place, he was reborn elsewhere, experiencing various karmic fruits according to his own actions.

“Great King, you should know that among the sentient beings of the world—whether virtuous or non-virtuous, superior or inferior—the fruit arises from its own cause without fail. Those who perform virtuous deeds have such actions as their destination and their reliance; at the time of death, they do not give rise to fear. When conditions here cease, they are born in another place to receive a superior karmic retribution.”
Therefore, Great King!

You should now abandon worldly dharmas and detach from all defiled attachments; cultivate supramundane practices and proceed toward the gateways of wholesome dharmas, maintaining the perception of impermanence in every moment of thought.
If it is thus, then within wholesome dharmas this is called diligence.
Furthermore, Great King, just as when people enter a great mass of fire, they must employ skillful means to immediately extinguish it;
When dwelling amidst the heat of affliction, one must rely upon purity to awaken;
when suffering from hunger and thirst, one can only be relieved by means of food and drink;
when tainted by the pain of illness, one can only be cured by means of excellent medicine.
In times of peril, one may escape all hardships only by encountering powerful and virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*);
when suffering from poverty, one can only be rescued by obtaining great wealth and treasures;
and when entering the ranks of battle, one must don brave and sturdy armor before victory in combat can be achieved.
"In all places, those who are without support or protection, solitary and afflicted by suffering, find their refuge only when they obtain friends.

Your Majesty! The supramundane wholesome dharmas are likewise; among all worldly things, they are like the aforementioned food, drink, excellent medicine, and friends, capable of providing support and protection."
"Great King!

If a person does not cultivate supramundane wholesome dharmas and has nothing upon which to rely, they will naturally give rise to fear at the time of death; who will be their savior? When they abandon this retribution and must undergo suffering themselves, who will rescue and deliver them? For these reasons, I speak according to reality."

"Great King! Swiftly abandon all views of permanence regarding worldly phenomena and cultivate the perception of impermanence; abandon views of solidity and cultivate the perception of disintegration, for they are like a mass of foam upon water and possess no reality. You should mindfully practice the supramundane wholesome dharmas, and having accomplished what you yourself must do, further exhort others to do the same; in this way, one is said to possess diligence within the wholesome dharmas."

"Great King! You should contemplate your own body: there is not even the slightest pleasure to be found therein. Although you are sustained by various kinds of superior, exquisite, and delicious food and drink, you have never for a single moment been free from the affliction of hunger and thirst. Thus, while it can temporarily sustain the life-faculty, once that karmic retribution of longevity is exhausted, it immediately disintegrates and returns to the law of impermanence."
"Great King!

Furthermore, observe your own person: although you possess various kinds of exquisite and wondrous robes, manifold ornaments, and even all manner of goods in your treasuries without any deficiency; and although you are fully equipped with the fourfold army of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, their number being so vast that none can equal it—even so, when the retribution of your life-span is exhausted, it all returns to impermanence."
"Furthermore, Great King! Suppose there is a person in the world who possesses great wealth;

day after day, they bathe themselves clean, anoint their bodies with fragrant oils, and adorn themselves with various exquisite garments, as well as wonderful flower garlands, strings of pearls, earrings, bracelets, and bangles. Having thus adorned themselves, they sit upon a precious throne, sovereign and majestic in their noble power, surrounded by their retinue. They play hundreds of thousands of kinds of exquisite music, and in every part of their magnificent jeweled pavilions, they burn sandalwood, aloeswood, and other fine incenses. These arise and cease in continuous succession, revolving without end, all because they are produced with ignorance as their cause."

From this, there arise various phenomena such as craving; if ignorance is extinguished, craving and the like do not arise. Once craving and the like have been extinguished, right practice can be established, and one becomes free from all faults—this is precisely what is called the supramundane dharma.
"Furthermore, Great King!
Regarding all objects of perception in the world— whether gained or lost, certain or uncertain,
desirable or undesirable— if a mind of craving arises without satiety, this constitutes a great loss."
"If one finds delight in and yearns for the Noble Path and supramundane dharmas without ever being satiated, this constitutes right practice and is of great benefit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Great King, you should now know: That nature of death is utterly evil;..."
That which can sever a person’s life-span and destroy the aggregates is a source of great terror;
it is not something the world desires or delights in.
When that nature of death arrives, it pervades all things.
In the sky and the great ocean, in deep caves and high mountains,
upon the earth and in all directions— nowhere can one escape.
Only those possessed of wisdom abide securely in the true Dharma.
Thus firm and unshakable, it cannot be destroyed by anything.
Before the retribution of one's lifespan has ended, one should exert great diligence,
extensively cultivate the causes of all virtues, and zealously practice the various holy conducts.
"By the power of these roots of goodness, one attains the realm of nirvāṇa;
having attained the realm of nirvāṇa, one is able to remain far removed from the fear of death.

At that time, the Great King Prasenajit of the Kingdom of Kośala, having heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, preach the sublime Dharma through various skillful means and parables, was filled with joy and exultation. He paid homage with reverence and praise, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and returned to his royal palace.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the great assembly of bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all filled with great joy; they accepted it with faith and practiced accordingly.

After King Jayasena had departed the city, he gradually made his way toward the Jeta Grove. There, the king immediately saw from afar the World-Honored One sitting serenely beneath a tree, surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus.
When the king saw him, he was filled with great joy; with deep faith and reverence, he descended from his chariot and removed his parasol.

Joining his palms and bowing low, he offered praise from afar: "The Buddha’s body is vast and expansive like a mountain of gold; his form is upright and majestic, peerlessly sublime. He possesses a great radiance like that of a hundred thousand suns, a blazing auspiciousness like a mass of fire. His faculties are tranquil and stilled as he abides in *śamatha*; adorned with all virtues, he is endowed with the *pāramitās*. With the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics fully perfected, he is a dragon among men, a lion among men, a great seer among men, and a victor among men—appearing in this world like a mountain of jewels."

At that time, having offered his praise, the Great King proceeded on foot to where the Buddha was. Upon reaching the Blessed One, he prostrated himself with his head at the World-Honored One’s feet and presented the Blessed One with such items as a jeweled crown, a jeweled parasol, a jeweled sword, a precious jewel, and jeweled sandals. Having made these offerings, he spoke thus:
“I pray only that the World-Honored One will accept what I have given.”
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted it.
The king then prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, withdrew to stand to one side, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will expound the essential Dharma for me, so that I may obtain great benefit and happiness throughout the long night.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the king, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Great King!
You have deep faith and reverence for the Tathāgata; you love, delight in, and seek the Buddha’s true Dharma; you are a truly virtuous man, endowed with pure goodness."

“As you have said that you wish to hear the essential points of the Dharma, you should listen attentively with proper mental attention; I shall proclaim it for you so that you may remember and practice it.
The Buddha said, “Great King!...”

You govern a great kingdom and are constantly honored and praised by hundreds of thousands of internal and external kinsmen; yet, despite such wealth, status, and sovereignty, when the retribution of your lifespan is exhausted, you will immediately experience suffering and distress, while all your retinue merely surround you in grief, lamentation, and weeping.

At that time, when one can no longer protect anything and life has come to an end, surrounded by internal and external relatives, one arrives at the Śītavana cemetery. There, all parts of the physical body disperse; skin, flesh, sinews, and bones are scattered in different places, and various insects and birds come to devour them. Once they have been consumed, this illusory body is entirely non-existent.
“Great King! For this reason, contemplate the world with discernment: what solidity or substance is there in it, which is like a mass of foam?

To conceive the notion of permanence regarding these impermanent and non-final dharmas is a perversion. All contaminated phenomena perish and dissolve moment by moment; observing this matter, I feel deep compassion.”
"Therefore, Great King, you must swiftly abandon all worldly dharmas and constantly mindfully practice the supramundane dharma. Why is this?

"Great King, you should know that all these phenomena of arising and ceasing have ignorance as their causal condition. That is to say: with ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair arise. Thus occurs this entire great mass of suffering."

When ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; when volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases; when consciousness ceases, name-and-form cease; when name-and-form cease, the six sense bases cease; when the six sense bases cease, contact ceases; when contact ceases, feeling ceases; when feeling ceases, craving ceases; when craving ceases, clinging ceases; when clinging ceases, existence ceases; when existence ceases, birth ceases; when birth ceases, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
"Therefore..."
